_comment: Shared SERVER-behaviour cases for the tag bus. Read by tools/check_protocol.py, which drives one running engine over the wire; tests/test_tag_parity.py points it at harness/engine_stub.py and `python tools/check_protocol.py` points it at the C# engine. The point is HP-19: engine/fixtures/tag_cases.json already pins the two Tag *models* together, but nothing pinned the two *servers* together, and all three divergences HP-18 closed lived in the server rather than the model. Cases name tags by role -- '@bit_output' and friends, resolved from the engine's own describe -- so the same file runs against any scene. A case whose roles the scene does not declare is skipped and reported as skipped, never silently passed: the sorting scene has no float tag at all, so float coverage means running this against a scene that does (res://templates/tank_level_control.json declares all six roles).
_roles: <type>_<kind>, e.g. bit_output, int_input, float_output. The first tag of each combination in the describe wins.
_scenarios: Most cases describe themselves entirely in prepare/write/force/raw/expect_* and are one connection and a burst of frames. The lifecycle half is choreography between two connections -- who gets refused, what a reconnect is told, which epoch a frame is stamped with -- so those cases name a 'scenario' instead, and tools/check_protocol.py's _SCENARIOS holds the runner for each. The first round of this file deliberately left that half out: HP-31 and HP-33 were about to reshape those same orderings, and pinning them before reshaping them would have pinned the bug. Both have landed.

cases.name: a bad bit does not take the rest of its batch with it
cases.why: HP-18.1. The C# server caught bad values per value and carried on; the Python stub let the coercion error escape its connection handler and DROPPED THE CONNECTION. One batch, two engines, two completely different outcomes.

cases.name: a bad bit at the head of a batch does not take the rest with it
cases.why: Same divergence, order reversed. JSON objects preserve order, so a bad value first is the case that aborted everything after it.

cases.name: the largest 32-bit integer is accepted
cases.why: HP-18.2. The boundary has to be on the same side of the line for both engines.

cases.name: one past the largest 32-bit integer is refused
cases.why: HP-18.2. Python accepted it into an unbounded int; C# threw OverflowException, which its per-value catch did not even name -- so the whole batch died and the sidecar was told nothing.

cases.name: the smallest 32-bit integer is accepted
one below the smallest 32-bit integer is refused
a float tag refuses a bit
NaN on the wire is refused and the connection survives
cases.why: HP-23. `NaN` is not JSON. Python's decoder read it anyway, so a non-finite value sailed into a float tag and out again as a payload the C# parser rejects; C# refused the frame but said nothing about it, so the sidecar believed its write had landed. Both must refuse it, both must say so, and neither may drop the connection.

cases.name: Infinity on the wire is refused and the connection survives
an overflowing float literal is refused
cases.why: HP-23 by the back door: 1e400 is perfectly legal JSON and decodes to infinity on both sides, so it never reaches the frame parser and has to be caught by the tag.

cases.name: a non-finite force is refused too
cases.why: HP-23. Forcing is the deliberate exception to the direction rule, not to the type rules.

cases.name: writing a simulator-owned input is refused by kind
a forced output reads as forced
cases.why: HP-13. The engine publishes `update` for inputs only, so without the observe channel a motor forced off while the PLC commands it on reads as on.

cases.name: a write underneath a force is absorbed, not observed
releasing a force reveals what the controller is commanding
a bad forced value is refused without dropping the connection
cases.why: `force` runs the same coercion as `write` and had the same escape route out of the Python stub's connection handler.

cases.name: an unknown tag in a batch is a warning, not an error
a frame that is not JSON at all is refused, not fatal
an epoch that is a string is refused, not guessed at
cases.why: HP-19. The epoch stamp is the engine's only defence against a frame in flight across a scene change, so a frame that does not carry a usable one cannot be acted on -- the engine cannot tell current from stale. C# threw out of GetValue<int>() into its catch-all and answered bad_message with a .NET type name in it; Python dropped the same frame in silence. Same frame, two answers.

cases.name: an epoch with a fractional part is refused by both, not applied by one
cases.why: HP-19, and the worse half of it. Python compares 3.0 == 3 as true, so a write stamped with a fractional epoch was APPLIED by one engine and refused by the other. Nothing in the protocol makes 3.0 an epoch.

cases.name: a write carrying no epoch at all is refused
cases.why: HP-19. Both engines used to drop this without a word, which is the one outcome that teaches a driver author nothing: `docs/tag-bus.md` says the sidecar must stamp every write, and a write that did not is a bug in the sidecar rather than a stale frame.

cases.name: a force with an unusable epoch is refused the same way a write is
cases.why: HP-19. Forcing is the deliberate exception to the direction rule, not to the epoch rule: a force in flight across a scene change pins whichever tag inherited the id.

cases.name: the greeting is hello then describe, each carrying exactly its fields
cases.why: HP-19, lifecycle. This is what would have caught FF-10 -- `hello` silently missing `tick_ms` while the sidecar filled in a default -- and until now it only ran from the CLI, against whichever engine the CLI was pointed at. As a case it runs against both.

cases.name: a second sidecar is told why it is being refused
cases.why: HP-19, lifecycle. Only one sidecar may connect -- two drivers writing the same output tag is a bug, not a feature -- but 'refused' has to mean the same thing on both engines. The C# server tore the TCP connection down before the websocket handshake finished, so the second sidecar saw 'did not receive a valid HTTP response' and could not tell 'another driver has it' from 'the engine is not running'. engine_stub has always completed the handshake and answered with a status. The refused client must also never be handed the tag set or an epoch, and the sidecar that was there first must keep its session.

cases.name: a sidecar that vanished without closing does not lock the next one out
cases.why: HP-19, lifecycle. A crash is not an orderly close, and the engine's idea of who is connected is only as fresh as its last poll. The C# server checked that idea BEFORE refreshing it, so the first reconnect after a crash was refused as a second sidecar -- 15 of 15 attempts, every one recovering only on the following frame. engine_stub answered the same reconnect immediately.

cases.name: reconnecting re-describes: same tags, a fresh epoch, the values kept
cases.why: HP-19, lifecycle. A sidecar coming back is handed the truth and not a blank table: whatever the last controller wrote is still what the machine is doing, and the epoch it is given must be one no earlier frame can pass for.

cases.name: a write stamped with the epoch from before the last describe is dropped
cases.why: HP-19, epoch semantics, over the wire rather than simulated: a reconnect IS a re-describe. Without the stamp, a write in flight across a scene change lands on whatever tag inherited that id. The case then sends the same write with the epoch it was actually given, so it cannot pass against an engine that has simply stopped accepting writes.

cases.name: a force stamped with a stale epoch is dropped too
cases.why: HP-19. A stale force is worse than a stale write: it pins the tag that inherited the id, and nothing clears it because nobody knows it is there.
